pos.personaBrief: Bukovi and Sebes wanted 'many movements, short passes, changing positions, speed' (Nemzeti Sport), and the FA Year Book describes ball control 'amounting to elegance'. That is a Danubian side built on keeping the ball, though it also used long passes.

pro.personaBrief: Short passing with flexible positioning, but 'they did not drop the long pass' and the play was 'a mingling of short and long passes'. Bozsik's 'piercing through-balls' show a willingness to take risks going forward.

est.personaBrief: The structure was relational: Hidegkuti dropped deep as a false nine, the forwards interchanged ('If I went forward, Puskás dropped back'), the wingers tucked in, and 'socialist football' meant every player could play anywhere. Zakariás was the one fixed holding role.

lar.personaBrief: UEFA has 'wingers who could slot into midfield' and Guide to Football has 'wingers tucked in to support the inside forwards'. The attack was concentrated through the middle, around Hidegkuti, Puskás, Kocsis and Bozsik.

blo.personaBrief: Buzánszky recalled that on losing the ball 'there were no empty spaces', so the team won it back quickly, and Puskás said 'in defence it was the same'. The shape itself was more defensive than the WM, with Zakariás screening the back three.

mar.personaBrief: No source covers marking. In a WM-derived era the three defenders probably picked up opposing forwards, and Sebes's opponent-specific preparation points towards direct individual duties.

pla.personaBrief: Sebes had a clear identity ('players and tactics to compete with anyone') but prepared in great detail for each opponent: English balls, a pitch with Wembley's dimensions, clubs imitating the next opponent. That preparation served his own system rather than replacing it.

res.personaBrief: 'We had done what we had to do, and we had done it in style' pairs result with style, but Sebes made 'a political issue of every important match' and defeat was not tolerated. The team always played to win.

sis.personaBrief: 'The system always trumped the individual', and 'socialist football' meant equal responsibility for every player. Sebes was an organiser who chose malleable players to fit the collective.

jog.personaBrief: The team played 'superb technical and tactical football' (Glanville), and Sebes added swimming for lung power. That was fitness work on top of technique, never a replacement for it.

bas.personaBrief: After Prague in 1949 he 'did away with the established stars' for 'youthful, malleable fresh faces like Kocsis and Czibor'. He built the core by concentrating players at Honvéd through the army takeover, not by developing them in an academy.

lid.personaBrief: Sebes was an authoritarian, political organiser with a 'rather strict timetable' and holistic control over the players' lives (museums instead of drinking). He still held regular tactical discussions that 'usually included input from captain Puskás'.
